controlsMoving.title: Controls: Moving Around
controlsMoving.description:
Move: arrow keys or WASD. Confirm and talk: Z or Enter. Cancel and pause menu: X or Escape. Run: hold Shift.

Running costs AP:

- a full AP meter is about ninety seconds of running
- walking refills AP slowly, standing still refills it fast
- running is never blocked, but AP also pays for battle skills

Z acts on whatever you face: a person, a door, a sign, an item on the ground, a workbench. Z on a party member opens their Empathize sheet.

C kicks, always with the foot, whatever weapon is equipped. Kicking breaks crates and barrels, forces doors and shoves movable objects. A kickable event makes a sound; silence means it cannot be kicked. A locked door takes seven to fifteen kicks. A target with a wall behind it is thrown behind you instead.

controlsMenus.title: Controls: Menu Hotkeys
controlsMenus.description:
Tab opens and closes the menu. Each screen also has its own letter, pressed on the map:

- I inventory
- C character sheet
- R equipment
- P magic and skills
- J quest log
- M minimap toggle
- B build (furniture and structures)
- V vehicles
- F factions
- H holdings (assets, property, portfolio)
- K cooking
- L this book
- N training
- Y bestiary
- U biologics
- O options
- G sandbox (tester builds only)

Inside the menu: 1 Thinker, 2 multiplayer, 3 Hypernet. On the map, 1 to 9 use the quick bar slots.

Reserved, so they cannot be bound to a menu: W, A, S, D (move), Z and X (confirm, cancel), Q and E (world map zoom), T (world map / local map).

F9 quicksave. F10 quickload. F11 fullscreen.

controlsMouse.title: Controls: Mouse
controlsMouse.description:
The mouse does not move your character.

- click and drag: pan the camera, it snaps back when you move with the keyboard
- wheel: zoom, world map only (+ and - do the same)
- hover an event: shows its label
- hold Alt: labels every event on screen

In battle: left click an enemy to use the selected command on it, right click to cycle to the next command, wheel to scroll the command list, 1 to 5 to pick and fire a command.

Menu pages are clickable throughout. The wheel scrolls whichever pane the cursor is over.

controlsGamepad.title: Controls: Controller
controlsGamepad.description:
A controller works everywhere, menus, star map and 3D minigames included.

- left stick: move, navigate lists
- right stick: pan the camera on the map
- R3: label every event on screen
- L2 / R2: zoom the world map, scroll long character creation overlays
- L1 / R1: cycle tabs in a menu, change character where there is a party switcher, arm and step the quick bar on the map

One thing needs a mouse: opening a search field. The magnifier handle is not focusable, so a pad walking a list never lands in a text box.

controlsRemap.title: Controls: Remapping
controlsRemap.description:
Options, Commands page. Keyboard and gamepad are remapped separately.

Every default command can be rebound, plus the ones this game adds:

- Zoom In: Q, LB
- Zoom Out: E, RB
- Kick: C, RT
- Run: Shift, LT

Bindings are stored with your settings and persist between sessions.

controlsScreen.title: What Is On The Screen
controlsScreen.description:
The party HUD sits top left, on the map and in battle. One row per member: name and level, HP bar with the number inside it, AP orb, MP bar. The acting member's card is lit and carries a caret.

A column of chips runs beside each card:

- on the map: hunger, sleep, hygiene, cravings, illness
- in battle: stat changes (STR 1.4x), class resources (pins, combo, chi), active states
- statuses appear in both

A chip appears when a value needs attention, in one colour past the warning line and a louder one past the critical line.

While the party is riding, the vehicle takes a row above the crew: condition as an HP bar, fuel where magic would be.

The quick bar sits bottom centre: favourite items on the map, the acting member's skills in battle.

Notifications appear top left as parchment cards. Transient ones fade; standing ones (overencumbered, hunted, poisoned) stay up while they are true.

The HUD can be turned off in Options, Video, or on the first step of character creation.

controlsSearch.title: Searching Inside Menus
controlsSearch.description:
Every long list carries the same search strip, this book included. It starts collapsed as a magnifier at the top of the page; click it and the caret goes into the field.

- while typing, the field owns the keyboard and no menu hotkey fires
- Escape empties the field, Escape again leaves it
- closing the magnifier discards the query

The main menu search covers more than one screen at once: carried items, gear worn by companions, skills (one row per member who knows them), recipes you can make with what you carry, bestiary creatures.

savingGame.title: Saving, Autosave and Quicksaves
savingGame.description:
The game autosaves on map change, at most once every few minutes, into an ordinary save slot.

F9 quicksaves, F10 quickloads. Quicksaves rotate over three dedicated slots. Any playthrough may overwrite any quicksave.

Deleting a permadeath savegame still leaves its diary behind for the next playthrough.

worldsFolders.title: Worlds and Savegames
worldsFolders.description:
A world is a folder, and several worlds can sit side by side. Worlds are made from the Worlds screen on the title menu. Until one exists, Explore, Reconnect, Story Mode and Sandbox stay greyed out.

A world is generated once, in full, before it is played: a century of history, the people and their homes and jobs, shop rotas, the dungeon layout, politics, faction accords, the settlement web, continental epidemics.

Every playthrough started in the same world walks into the same place, already changed by the ones before it: emptied chests, planted crops, market prices, bashed doors, built furniture. The clock only moves forward, so loading a save continues from the latest date reached there.

Other playthroughs appear in person, standing where they were last saved.

optionsMenu.title: Options
optionsMenu.description:
Options is split into tabs. Plugins add rows to these tabs instead of opening menus of their own.

- Video: resolution, fullscreen, pixel perfect scaling, retro shader, UI and font scaling, party HUD on or off
- Audio: volumes as percentages, battle music picker
- Gameplay: party formation (Close or Loose), auto idle explorer, world map hints
- Commands: keyboard and gamepad remapping, separately
- Experimental: includes the local language model that can write NPC dialogue in place of the Markov chains

Fullscreen turns itself on the first time a distributed build runs. After that your setting is kept.

modsUpdates.title: Mods and Updates
modsUpdates.description:
The game reads a mods folder next to the executable. Each subfolder is one mod and mirrors the game's folder structure, so a mod can replace a data file, add a picture or add new content. Mods need the desktop build.

In the Mod Manager: Enter toggles a mod, arrows move it in the load order. Mods at the bottom load last and win.

The title screen has an Updates entry. It compares your files against the build's and downloads only what differs.

- nothing is moved into place until every file is downloaded and checked
- replaced files are backed up first
- the game must be closed and reopened to load the new files
- two channels, stable and unstable, and any earlier build can be restored
- a build marked as a major update cannot be patched across, and the whole game is offered instead

partyBasics.title: The Party
partyBasics.description:
Party size: 3. The first member is the leader. The leader is the one you steer, the one whose needs drain fastest and the one NPCs react to.

A fourth companion (pet, follower or child) walks along without being a member. It never fights and cannot be hurt or targeted.

Each member has their own needs, opinions, reputation, specializations and relationships with the other two.

Formation, set in Options:

- Close: everyone walks in the leader's footsteps
- Loose (default): the others move on their own and only regroup when left off screen

A loose party acts on its own between walks: standing and thinking, looking at things, talking to townspeople or to each other. Any meter below 35% sends that member off to eat, wash, play, talk or rent a room out of the party purse. Every action is announced.

Run for two seconds to call everyone into the column. Walking does not.

Face a companion and press confirm to open their Empathize sheet.

partyCreation.title: Making Your Characters
partyCreation.description:
Characters are made one at a time. Three routes:

- Quick: look, class, traits, gear
- Dossiers: pre-made characters. Some are reusable in any world, the rest are spent once used. A dossier may bring its own vehicle, background, hometown and alternate skins
- Detailed: the full sheet in the Empathize panel. Humanoid or creature, name, gender, class, level, portrait, sprite, age, nation, traits, specializations, personality, ideology, faction, wealth, morality, orientation, reproduction, backstory reroll

Closing a sheet moves on to the next member.

Starting gear is picked by price, not power. The starter weapon pool is the cheapest weapon of each type, and each class loadout fits a fixed budget. Trait gear is granted separately, exactly as the trait says.

partyClasses.title: Classes
partyClasses.description:
A class sets starting stats, the skill schools you learn fastest, and a favoured element.

Each class names primary and secondary skill categories:

- primary: progression 3x, skills cost half
- secondary: progression 1.5x, full price
- outside your curriculum: needs a skill already known in it, triple price

Training lists only your own curriculum. Outside skills are still learnable, just not shelved for you.

Any class can equip any weapon. Skill with a weapon is a trainable proficiency instead (see the equipment pages).

Creature classes are a separate set: Feral, Mimic, Monster, Mana Cyborg, Ghost, Zombie, Mutant, Drone. A character on one of them is an animal, not a person.

partyTraits.title: Traits
partyTraits.description:
Traits are bought at creation from a pool of trait points. Positive traits cost points, negative traits pay points back, so drawbacks fund virtues.

Traits change base stats and grant skills, items and equipment. They are also read during play:

- NPC first impressions: compatible traits give a standing bonus, incompatible ones a penalty
- how much anyone minds your condition. A Germaphobe reacts to filth nearly three times as hard as an ordinary person, a Feral character not at all
- which specializations start with a head start
- what companions do with their free time and what they say

Traits are permanent and cannot be respecced.

partyAttributes.title: Attributes
partyAttributes.description:
Six attributes:

- STR: carrying capacity, physical damage
- CON: damage absorbed, how long a choke is held
- DEX: speed, precision, evasion, escaping holds
- INT: learning, mathematical schools of magic
- WIS: judgement, resistance, intuitive schools
- PSI: luck. Enemy reactions when talked to, loot rolls, hidden rolls in your favour

The status sheet shows them as medallions with current modifiers. The battle HUD shows the modifier as a multiplier (STR 1.4x).

partyCreatures.title: Playing A Creature
partyCreatures.description:
A party member can be a creature. The creature builder uses one archetype, or two crossed, plus a battler and a sprite.

The archetype drives the body: the limb and organ system gives the creature exactly the parts of that species, with its reach, its number of hands and its weak points.

- creature class: non-sentient. No conversation, no politics, no savings, no property
- civilised class: a person shaped like an animal, treated as a person everywhere

Anatomy is mechanical, not cosmetic. It sets how many weapons can be held, whether any can be held, whether you can be choked, and what a pregnancy produces.

partyPortraits.title: Portraits and 3D Models
partyPortraits.description:
Each character is drawn one of three ways, chosen at creation and never mixed:

- bust: hand drawn portrait
- model: procedural 3D body. Six anatomical slots (head, torso, two arms, two legs) can each take the matching part of any registered creature. Height, build, head size, ears, nose and skin are sliders; fangs, horns, tail, wings and halo are toggles
- sprite: used by monsters, creatures built on an existing species, recruited enemies and summons. Always shown as the 3D model of their species

The choice is used by the status screen, the dialogue busts and the Empathize panel.

partyRecruiting.title: Recruiting People
partyRecruiting.description:
Three ways into the party:

- talk a monster round during battle
- ask a townsperson through the Empathize panel, once they think well enough of the member asking
- adopt a creature as a pet or follower and train it up

A recruited townsperson leaves the map for good: their event is removed and their profile, personality, traits, skills, wealth, history and standing with everyone else all move into the party actor.

The party holds three, so someone must leave for someone to join. Retired members go back to the dossier board and can be recalled later.

partyPets.title: Pets, Followers and Children
partyPets.description:
A fourth companion follows the party without being a member. It never fights, cannot die and cannot be targeted.

- follower: a creature recruited from a monster that talks
- pet: one recruited from a monster that does not
- child: the result of a pregnancy. It wears the bearing parent's sprite and gets a generated name

Only one walks with you at a time. The Followers page lists all of them and can swap or release them.

Pets and followers can be trained into party members. The species roster decides which classes are available: a talker is never trained into a beast class, and a species with no roster falls back to Beast, or Freelancer if it talks.

- training is measured in world clock minutes, which only pass while you play
- Animal Training (Leadership for a talker) shortens it
- only the companion currently walking with you makes progress
- children and summons are never trained

partyReproduction.title: Reproduction and Pregnancy
partyReproduction.description:
Every body has a reproductive type, set at creation from the species:

- Testicles: fertility, sperm count, motility and morphology are simulated and respond to hormones and body condition
- Uterus: a 28 day cycle, fertile on days 12 to 16. Biologics shows the cycle day and current fertility
- Oviparous: a clutch of one to four eggs
- Plant: seeds develop one after another, endlessly, and stockpile until planted
- Mitosis: the body divides and produces a copy of itself

A pregnancy runs for the term of the species. Biologics shows gestational age and fetal stage. Symptoms arrive as states, and heart rate rises.

Newborns register in the Followers menu as children with their own name and the parent's face. Every hatchling of a clutch registers. Mitosis produces a copy, not a child.

Pregnancy, birth and division are all written into the party diary.

partyDeath.title: Death, Gravestones and Permadeath
partyDeath.description:
Falling in battle is not automatic death. Health protection and danger warnings let you break off, and fleeing always works.

A dead character leaves a gravestone where they fell. The grave stays on the map, can be found again, and is where restoration is performed.

Permadeath: the character is gone for good and their quicksaves go with them. A wiped party ends that party only; the next one starts in the same changed place.

Lost limbs are not death and are not fixed by healing (see the body pages).

partyBanterPage.title: What Your Companions Say
partyBanterPage.description:
Two or more companions hold discussions of two to four lines, drawn from what is happening:

- a recent event nobody has commented on yet, usually a purchase
- everyone below 40% health
- any member with a meter below 35%
- a diary line from the last few hours: a fight won, an artifact found, a floor descended, a member joined
- the biome family they are standing in
- the road, the money, the leader, the plan
- one personality opening and another answering

A third member's personality often closes the exchange, so the same script reads differently depending on who is present.

The same purchase draws different reactions: the disciplined member resents the cost, the hedonist asks why only one was bought, the cautious one asks what the party now lacks.

They also talk while driving, with bubbles over the vehicle, and on trains, coaches and taxis. A party of one talks to itself.

partyAutoIdle.title: The Auto Explorer
partyAutoIdle.description:
An Options toggle lets the game play itself while you are idle. The party explores, crosses the map and looks after its own needs, as a loose companion does.

It takes the same steps and pays the same costs you would, and returns control as soon as you press anything.

progressLevels.title: Levels and Experience
progressLevels.description:
Experience comes from winning fights. A level raises the six attributes and the HP and MP pools.

Levels are a small part of power. What matters more:

- skills learned, which cost knowledge, not experience
- specializations trained, which cost use
- gear carried, and proficiency with it
- the condition of the body

progressKnowledge.title: Knowledge Points
progressKnowledge.description:
Knowledge points (KP) buy skills. KP belongs to the party, not to one member.

Earned from:

- winning fights, scaled against the party's median level, so weak enemies pay almost nothing
- finishing quests
- resolving a procedural adventure well
- dreams
- scanning objects with the Raman spectroscope

Skill prices are computed from combat value: MP and AP cost first, then damage scaling, flat damage, repeats, targets hit and inflicted states.

- weakest skill: 50 KP
- ordinary skill: a few hundred
- strongest ordinary skill: a couple of thousand
- Esoteric: ten times its score
- Forbidden: a hundred times its score

Primary school halves the price, secondary pays full, outside schools triple it. Nothing costs less than 50 KP.

progressAtlas.title: The Atlas of Circles
progressAtlas.description:
Skills are laid out as a sphere grid. Each school is an alchemical circle: concentric rings from its weakest working outward to its strongest, joined by spokes, with upgrade spurs on the rim ending in esoteric workings.

- you can only buy a skill adjacent to one you know
- one known neighbour is enough; links are alternatives, never joint requirements
- the innermost ring of every school is always open

Forbidden workings sit alone in the centre, connected to nothing. The whole school must be known before any of them opens; after that, any one can be taken first.

One school is shown at a time. Use the pager on the header bar or walk off the rim to left or right. Wheel and Shift zoom, drag pans, selecting a skill opens its sheet.

progressTraining.title: Training and Progression
progressTraining.description:
Each member trains one skill at a time, tracked per person.

- winning a battle: 3 points
- using a skill of the same category in battle: 2 points

Primary categories multiply this by 3, secondary categories by 1.5.

progressSpecializations.title: Specializations
progressSpecializations.description:
About eight hundred specializations, from Wrestling to Accounting to Beekeeping. Each is governed by one attribute and has five tiers: Untrained, Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, Master.

A specialization's level is the highest of three sources: trained through play, granted by class, granted by a trait. Changing class or taking a trait shows on the sheet immediately.

They train by doing. Cooking raises cooking, wrestling raises wrestling, selling raises haggling. The leader earns full value, anyone else present earns 35%. The first tier costs 3 points.

They are read across the whole game: forging quality, lockpicking, hold damage, what a merchant accepts, whether a recipe can be read at all.

progressPassives.title: Class Passives
progressPassives.description:
Every class has signature passives. They need no slot and no activation. Some work in combat, some only outside it.

They are listed on the status sheet under Passives.

progressLoadout.title: The Nine Skill Slots
progressLoadout.description:
A character can carry nine skills into a fight, out of everything they know. The skill menu is tabbed by role, and the nine chosen fill the battle quick bar.

Everything known stays known. Changing the loadout is free between fights.

progressFusion.title: Fusing Spells
progressFusion.description:
From the Magic page, two abilities can be forged into a new one.

- dominant slot: a spell you know. It sets the result's damage, scope, hit type and icon
- recessive slot: a spell or a skill. A skill makes the result a skill, otherwise it stays magic
- any named animation can be chosen, previewable in 3D

The fusion costs the sum of its parts in MP and AP, and is paid for in the sum of the components' teaching prices in KP. The components are forgotten on fusing, and the fusion can be split back into them at any time.

progressGrimoires.title: Grimoires and Skill Books
progressGrimoires.description:
A grimoire offers five random workings and lets one reader claim one. The five are rolled once when the book is opened, against the whole party, and switching reader does not reroll them.

A reader can only claim an offer whose MP cost fits their maximum MP and that they do not already know. The rest are greyed out.

The party's median PSI raises the chance of a Forbidden working appearing among the five.

Variants: school specific grimoires, category specific skill books, and the Forbidden Grimoire, which offers nothing else.

progressBladeSeeds.title: Blade Seeds
progressBladeSeeds.description:
Twelve seeds, one per weapon type. A seed is a permanent upgrade path for a whole weapon type rather than for a single weapon.

It grows as that weapon type is used, and what it grows into is procedural, so no two worlds grow the same blade. A seed outlasts the weapon that carried it.

gearSlots.title: Equipment: Hands and Slots
gearSlots.description:
There is no dual wield flag. Weapon slots come from anatomy: every body part the species declares as able to hold a weapon is a slot. Hands take a weapon or a shield without distinction, so two shields are as legal as two swords.

- a two handed weapon needs two free hands
- with one hand: one one handed weapon or one shield, and no other weapon slot
- a body with no hands holds its weapon in the mouth: one slot, anything fits. The samurai class keeps a mouth slot on top of its hands
- maximum eight weapon slots, however many limbs a body has
- past two weapons each parameter becomes the median of what is carried, and two weapons picked at random swing each turn
- losing a limb removes its slot and drops what it held

gearProficiency.title: Weapon Proficiency
gearProficiency.description:
Any class can equip any weapon type.

Skill with a weapon is a specialization, one per weapon type, twelve in all. It starts at Intermediate for the types your class was once limited to and Untrained for everything else, and it scales the weapon's parameters:

- Untrained 33%
- Beginner 67%
- Intermediate 100%
- Advanced 110%
- Master 125%

Winning a battle grants one proficiency point per equipped weapon type.

gearScaling.title: What a Weapon Scales On
gearScaling.description:
A weapon does not always scale on STR. Its attack skill sets the attribute it reads, and the equip screen names it when the weapon slot is selected.

- no attack skill: STR
- otherwise DEX, INT, WIS, CON, PSI, or a mix of two

gearArmor.title: Armour and Derived Stats
gearArmor.description:
Equipment feeds four out of combat stats besides defence:

- clothes: Substance and Stealth
- robes: Arcane
- light armour: Stealth
- heavy armour: Intimidation

Weapons feed them too: daggers and bows give Stealth; swords, heavy weapons, axes and claws give Intimidation; staves give Arcane; whips, projectiles and guns give Substance.

They are read outside combat: how people answer you, what a guard assumes, which approaches are open.

gearModifiers.title: Modifiers on Gear
gearModifiers.description:
A weapon or armour piece can carry one modifier, which changes its stats, price and traits:

- Sharp: raises STR and price. Weapons only
- Refined: raises CON and WIS and price. Any equipment
- Poisoned: adds poison, changes price. Weapons only
- Worn: lowers CON, WIS and price. Armour only

The modifier is part of the item and moves with it.

gearWeight.title: Weight and Encumbrance
gearWeight.description: Every item has a weight and the party has a carry capacity. Going over it raises a standing notification that stays up until you are back under.

gearBackpack.title: The Backpack
gearBackpack.description:
The backpack is tabbed by category: food, medical, tools, weapons, armour, materials. It shows the weight readout, the item detail card and the favourites bar.

Nine favourite slots hold usable items and share the quick bar with battle skills.

- on the map, 1 to 9 use the item in that slot; an item that must be given asks who
- in the backpack, the same keys assign the inspected item to a slot
- items can be dragged onto slots, right click clears one

Only usable items can be favourited. Weapons and armour are equipped instead.

gearArtifacts.title: Artifacts
gearArtifacts.description:
Artifacts are procedurally generated items, weapons and armour, each named and unique.

The Artifact Analyzer on the Hypernet reads what an unfamiliar one does.

gearContainers.title: Containers and Storage
gearContainers.description:
Chests, cupboards, crates and sacks store items and can be emptied or filled at will.

The party's own storage travels with it: the extradimensional container, and the holds of the camper and the car.

gearRarity.title: Loot and Rarity
gearRarity.description:
Random loot is scaled against the party's median level, not the leader's.

Items are printed in their rarity colour everywhere: reward popup, backpack, shop counter. A haul of several items keeps its popup on screen longer.

Item descriptions are combinatorial, resolved from the world seed: the same sword reads the same way all through one world and differently in the next.

needsOverview.title: The Five Needs
needsOverview.description:
Every person in the world, your party included, carries five meters:

- Hunger
- Sleep
- Hygiene
- Company
- Fun

All five run from 100 to 0 and drain as time passes. Time passes as you walk: one minute per ten steps on an ordinary map, ten minutes per tile on the world map, two minutes per tile in a vehicle.

The leader drains fastest. Running drains everything faster.

They show as chips beside each party card, in one colour below 20% and a louder one at 0. The main menu draws them in full, and every change is announced with the party median: "Fun 62% up +8".

At 0: hunger drains HP, sleep drains MP, the rest cost you socially and mentally.

Augments can slow a need, stop it, or reverse it. A ruminant stomach burns less, a somnologic regulator never tires, a self cleaning dermis gains hygiene as you walk.

needsHunger.title: Hunger and Nutrition
needsHunger.description:
Every edible item carries calories, fat and protein, and eating credits all three. What a meal is worth depends on its contents, not its price.

- hunger can pass 100, up to a ceiling of 150%
- above 110% you are overfed, which is a state with penalties
- above 100 hunger burns three times faster

Temperature costs food at both ends: cold burns calories for warmth, heat raises metabolism. The travel card shows the ambient temperature.

At 0 hunger you take continuous HP damage until you eat.

Food is bought, foraged, grown, hunted and cooked. A cooked meal's nutrition is the sum of its ingredients.

needsSleep.title: Sleep, Rest and Time Awake
needsSleep.description:
Two separate values are tracked.

- the sleep meter: how tired you feel. Coffee or a sit down refills it. At 0 it drains MP
- time since you last slept: a stamp on the world clock that only a night's rest clears. It reads zero up to a day awake, climbs through two days, and maxes at a week

Time since sleep is what turns dreams hostile and pulls the party's mind apart.

Beds, campfires, tents and world map camps open the rest menu. Sleep refills the meter completely whatever hour you wake at. Wait, and the T hotkey, only advance the clock and never rest the party.

Cryogenic sleep is separate: pick a year to wake in and the world moves on without you.

A long rest can drop the party into a dream (see the dream page).

needsHygiene.title: Hygiene, and What It Costs You
needsHygiene.description:
Hygiene drains slightly faster than sleep. Refill it at a washroom, bathroom, shower, sink or fountain. Loose party members go and find one below 35%.

Hygiene changes what people think of you, and it works both ways: your hygiene is read against the person you talk to, and theirs against you.

- at 60% and above nobody notices
- below 60%, each point costs a little under half a point of standing
- the penalty caps at 45 opinion points

Traits set how much it matters. Feral ignores it entirely, Ascetic barely notices; Street Urchin, Cave Dweller, Survivalist, Farmer and Veteran mind little. Proud, Wealthy, Beautiful, Perfectionist, Noble, Hypochondriac and Germaphobe mind a lot, the Germaphobe nearly three times as much as an ordinary person. Several such traits multiply; one "does not notice" trait overrides everything.

Courting reads both bodies a second time at a heavier weight, on top of the standing already lost. The panel names which of the two needs a bath.

needsSocial.title: Company
needsSocial.description:
Company drains like any other need and is refilled by talking: to townspeople, or between two of your own members.

A loose member starved of company walks up to someone and starts a conversation unprompted. That conversation moves what the other person thinks of that member, up or down, and hygiene counts in it.

Gaining standing with someone feeds the social meter of the member who gained it.

needsLeisure.title: Fun
needsLeisure.description:
Fun is refilled by playing: arcade cabinets, pianos, pool tables, card games, and jokes that land in conversation.

A joke that lands also raises the listener's Fun for the rest of the day.

A party with Fun on the floor complains about it in banter.

needsAddiction.title: Cravings and Withdrawal
needsAddiction.description:
Five traits are dependencies: alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, narcotics and gambling. Only a member with one of those traits has a craving meter.

A craving runs backwards: it climbs while unfed. 0 is just satisfied, 100 is withdrawal. Feeding it drops it to 0.

Withdrawal starts at a full meter and only lifts once the craving is well below it, so one dose does not clear it.

Cravings climb more slowly during sleep, and always on the member carrying the trait, never on the leader.

bodyParts.title: Limbs and Organs
bodyParts.description:
Every character and monster has individual limbs and organs, each with its own health, taken from its species archetype.

Damage is spread across parts. A part at 0 is destroyed, carries a permanent penalty while it stays that way, and changes what the body can do:

- a lost hand takes its weapon slot and drops what it held
- a body with no hands holds a weapon in its mouth
- damaged legs cost movement and evasion
- vital organs are shielded from ordinary damage and only exposed by deliberate targeting or by a state that opens them

A part at 0, damaged or severed can neither grapple nor be grappled.

Parts never heal on their own. They are treated at a clinic, restored by magic, or replaced with a prosthetic. In Blood and Oil mode a slashing blow can take a part off the body, carrying its augment with it, while a part that is only broken still mends under a potion or a spell.

The status sheet has an Anatomy section showing the whole body part by part.

bodyBiologics.title: Biologics
bodyBiologics.description:
Biologics is the deep readout: vital signs, hormones, blood chemistry, brain regions and their activity, blood type, reproductive cycle, and every condition acting on the body.

Heart rate responds to what is happening to you. Hormones respond to sleep, injury and pregnancy. Blood type is set once, by choice or rolled from the name, and never changes.

The Ley Vein system links it to limb damage: blockages appear here when the body has been hurt.

healthDiseases.title: Diseases
healthDiseases.description:
Hundreds of diseases exist. Each has a transmission chance, one or more vectors (airborne, saliva, bite, contact, sexual and others), stat modifiers while carried, and often a state that only appears after the carrier has walked a set number of steps. That delay is the window period.

Transmission:

- between your own members: rolled each time you open the pause menu
- between the party and a townsperson: rolled each time you open their Empathize panel
- venereal diseases never spread by proximity, only between romantic partners

Every NPC carries a medical history seeded from the world, with past diseases and lasting conditions such as badly set bones, readable on the Health tab of their panel.

Diagnose examines the whole party and names every illness carried, window period included. It works in battle and on the map.

healthEpidemics.title: Epidemics
healthEpidemics.description:
A continental epidemic model runs above individual illness, whether or not you are watching it.

- each infected town runs its own curve, resolved one day at a time at midnight
- cases export to other towns along map distance, with occasional long jumps
- public response builds the longer a town has been infected, and eventually breaks the wave

Two kinds: a medical outbreak, a pathogen with a case fatality ratio, and a hysteria, which has none. Dancing fever, genital theft panics, phantom gassers. A hysteria is caught by witnessing it and spread by talking about it.

Every world starts with three outbreaks running: one hysteria, one ordinary medical outbreak, one rare and mortal one.

Anyone in an infected town is exposed, you included, and the people around you carry the local prevalence. Outbreaks move mood, hiring, shop traffic, need drain, gossip and the news.

The Eurodemics observatory on the Hypernet tracks all of it.

healthSurgery.title: Clinics, Prosthetics and Field Surgery
healthSurgery.description:
A clinic can install a body part, remove one, replace one or fit an implant.

- installing: 1000 euros per percent of body health the part represents
- removal: 100 euros per percent
- vital parts cannot be removed
- an installed part grants its stat bonus, removing it takes the bonus away

Field surgery is the same operation on the road. The party picks a patient and a surgeon, nothing is bought, only parts already carried can be fitted, an augment can be taken out but never seated, and there is no fee.

Every operation is a roll, with the odds shown beforehand:

- the surgeon's Surgery specialization: 35 / 50 / 65 / 78 / 90 percent by tier
- under a roof +10, in a cave -5, in the open -10
- rain -15, storm -25, snow +5
- operating on yourself -15

A failure wounds the patient elsewhere. Vital organs are only at risk in Blood and Oil mode, which is also the only mode where a part can leave the body, carrying its augment out.

healthAugments.title: Augments
healthAugments.description:
The Augments register has two lists.

- Fitted: every augment the party wears, with its wearer and socket
- Catalogue: everything that exists, readable before paying to have it grafted

The dossier gives the cost, the bonus, the skill it teaches with that skill's own description, and every socket that accepts it, creature sockets included.

Augments are also how the needs system is bent: the right hardware slows a meter, stops it, or reverses it.

healthWeatherBody.title: Weather, Temperature and the Body
healthWeatherBody.description:
Ambient temperature is a number, shown on the travel card, and it acts on the body:

- cold burns calories for warmth, so hunger drains faster
- heat raises metabolism, with the same result
- rain -15 and storms -25 to field surgery, snow +5
- weather drives what people do and where they are

combatBasics.title: How a Fight Starts
combatBasics.description:
There are no random encounters. Every monster stands on the map and carries its level over its head. You fight it by walking into it.

Turns are individual: each battler acts when its own turn comes up, in agility order, and your action resolves as soon as you choose it. There is no planning phase.

Enemies keep their damage between fights. A wounded monster you ran from is still wounded when you come back. Corpses stay on the map.

Fleeing always works.

combatCommands.title: The Battle Commands
combatCommands.description:
The command menu holds:

- Attack, with whatever is equipped. Cost, reach and scaling come from the weapon
- Guard
- Skills and Magic, holding the nine you carry
- Item
- Check: opens the enemy's body, every limb and organ, its condition and the chance of hitting it
- Target: aims your next blow at one part
- Wrestle: takes hold of the enemy (own page)
- Talk: another way to end a fight (own page)
- Reload, when a firearm is empty
- Escape

Wrestle and Talk are commands, not skills. They take no loadout slot, cannot be forgotten, and come from the body rather than the class.

Mouse: left click an enemy to run the selected command on it, right click to cycle commands, wheel to scroll them, keys 1 to 5 for the first five.

combatAP.title: MP and AP
combatAP.description:
Two resources.

MP is magic. Spells cost it and it refills slowly. Most rites and summons are held with it.

AP is momentum, capped at 100. It is spent by battle skills and by sprinting on the map, out of the same meter.

- running: a full meter in about ninety seconds
- walking: slow regeneration
- standing still: fast regeneration

Cost type follows ability type: magic is written in CamelCase, costs MP and sits under Magic; a skill is written in plain words, costs AP and sits under Skills.

combatBodyParts.title: Hitting What You Aim At
combatBodyParts.description:
Monsters have the same limbs and organs the party does, taken from their species.

Check lists every part with its condition and the chance to hit it. Target aims your next blow at one. The chance comes from the part's size, your weapon type read against your stats, and a random swing of plus or minus ten percent per part.

- destroying a limb removes what it does: a broken leg slows, a ruined wing stops flight, no hands means no weapon held
- vital organs cannot be reached by ordinary blows, only by a targeted attack

Part damage persists through the fight, and a finishing blow can sever the part.

combatDamageTypes.title: Damage Types & Piercing Mechanics
combatDamageTypes.description:
Every attack, skill, and weapon carries a Damage Type: Explosive, Piercing, Cutting, Blunt, Area, Abstract, or None.

Limb Severing & Spread:

- Explosive, Piercing, and Cutting can sever or amputate body parts on lethal blows. Blunt, Area, Abstract, and None damage break or ruin parts in place without severing
- Area and Explosive damage spread across multiple body parts (2 to 4 parts). Piercing, Cutting, Blunt, and Abstract concentrate 100% of damage onto a single targeted body part

Piercing Mechanics:

- Guard (Status 2): Piercing weapons, skills, and spells punch through guard, dealing half of full damage instead of heavy guard reduction
- Protect (Status 19 / Substitute): When an ally is protected by a substitute, piercing attacks strike the protector for full damage AND penetrate through to hit the protected ally for half damage
- Divine Shield (Status 32): Piercing attacks ignore Divine Shield completely, bypassing its 100% physical evasion and all elemental damage reduction
- Magic Reflection (Status 18): Piercing spells and skills pierce through reflection shields, hitting the target directly without being reflected

combatWrestle.title: Wrestling
combatWrestle.description:
Wrestle is available to any body with at least one limb whole enough to grip, against any enemy still standing. It costs nothing and is never learned.

Choosing it targets one enemy and replaces the command menu with the grapple plan. Three choices:

- which of your limbs takes the hold
- which of their limbs it is taken on
- which hold to use

Each row shows the odds. A separate window lists the whole body, the state of every part and what that limb can do. A part at 0 HP, damaged or severed can neither grab nor be grabbed, on either side.

The holds:

- Grapple, STR against DEX: takes hold. Everything else needs one first
- Strike, STR against DEX: needs no hold, and can concuss on the head
- Joint lock, DEX against STR: pins, often breaks the guard
- Wrench, STR against CON: heavy damage, can cause bleeding
- Slam, CON against DEX: guard broken, winded, chance to stun
- Choke, CON against CON, head only: guard broken, vitals exposed, chance to stun
- Rip, STR against CON: low odds, enormous damage, can tear the limb off

Everything scales with the Wrestling specialization, which trains by wrestling.

Any trained martial art adds its own moves to the finisher shelf without them being learned as skills, listed with the art they come from and the odds of landing them.

combatTalk.title: Talking to Monsters
combatTalk.description:
A monster tagged as able to understand you can be talked to. Talk opens a panel with the odds of each approach printed beside it.

Every enemy carries a disposition from 1 to 100, rolled when it appears: 40% start at 10 to 40, 40% at 41 to 70, 20% at 71 to 100, shifted by species. Hurting it lowers disposition by 5 to 15 points depending on the blow.

Approaches:

- Chat, which builds rapport. Chance is disposition plus one fifth of the difference between your PSI and its own, floor 10%, cap 95%
- Surrender, same odds. It flees the fight
- Join the party, which needs a free slot. Above 80 disposition it uses the chat chance, below that a small chance, never under 5%
- Follow you, or be adopted as a pet. A talker needs 70 disposition, an animal uses the ordinary chance
- Insult, which always lands and lowers disposition
- Throw a stone, which always works
- Pet it

Creatures marked as forces rather than people, petrodemons above all, refuse every approach.

A monster talked into joining becomes a party member. One taken as pet or follower walks behind the party and can be trained into a member later.

combatEnemyLevels.title: Enemy Levels and Where They Live
combatEnemyLevels.description:
The Enemy Spawn option sets how enemy levels are chosen. Three settings:

Balanced. Roaming enemies come from a band above the party's median level: median L meets L to L + 7 + L/10. Level 1 meets 1 to 8, level 50 meets 50 to 62. One encounter per world tile is placed above the band as a boss, never over 100.

Distance from spawn, the default. The level is set by how far the world square lies from the square you started on: level 1 at home, the top of the roster at the far corner, a smooth climb between. Each square fields creatures whose habitat matches the biome and whose level falls in the ten level bracket of that place.

Chaos. The whole roster, flat random, level 1 to 110, redealt on every map entry.

No creature is exclusive to a country. Every nation holds every creature its biomes hold; the nation only changes how common each is.

The calendar sits above all three settings:

- 2001: the band as the mode sets it
- 2002 to 2009: the band climbs ten levels a year
- 2010 to 2011: no band. Anything from 1 to 110 roams
- 2012 onward: nothing below level 80, and no ceiling

combatMovementAI.title: How Monsters Behave
combatMovementAI.description:
Each roaming monster carries a movement personality that sets what it does while idle, how it notices you (sight range, facing cone, line of sight) and what it does once it has.

Personalities: Fixed, Random, Approach, Fleeing, Skittish, Grazer, Sentry, Guard, Patrol, Territorial, Ambusher, Lurker, Mimic, Swooper, Stalker, Hunter, Charger, Pack, Erratic, Drifter, Orbiter, Scavenger, Coward.

A Grazer never notices you. A Sentry has a cone and can be walked around. An Ambusher is not where it appears to be. A Stalker follows you. A Pack does not fight alone.

combatSafety.title: Danger Warnings and Surviving a Blow
combatSafety.description:
Before a fight, the party's median level is compared with the enemy and a warning appears when it is out of range. Enemy levels are drawn over their heads on the map.

Inside a fight, each character has one health protection charge per battle: the first blow that would kill them leaves them at 1 HP. It does not return until the next fight.

Blood and Oil mode removes the charge.

combatModes.title: Difficulty and Combat Modes
combatModes.description:
Several settings change what combat is. Most are chosen at character creation.

- Peaceful: monsters act only once hurt. An unprovoked enemy skips its turn with a line about what it is doing. Provocation is per enemy. A party wipe respawns you at your respawn point with nobody dead. Roaming monsters wander instead of chasing
- Ordinary: death leaves a gravestone and the run continues
- Hardcore and Blood and Oil: death is a game over with no respawn, and the character is removed. Blood and Oil also removes the health protection charge and lets a slashing blow take a part off the body, carrying its augment. A part it only breaks still heals
- Card combat: replaces the command menu (own page)
- Map battle: fights on the live map (own page)

combatMapBattle.title: Map Battle Mode
combatMapBattle.description:
An experimental option fights every battle on the map you are standing on instead of a battle screen.

- everyone fights from where they stand. Only a member off screen is placed, on a muster tile near the fight
- every other monster on the map keeps its position and behaviour. Any that wanders within a few tiles joins the fight, with its own HP card and turn slot
- a townsperson near the brawl joins your side if the party is well liked or if they are brave. They fight from their own profile: level, stats, skills, pockets
- Move lets the acting battler reposition before acting, with a range driven by agility
- weapons have reach: 1 for melee, 2 for spears, whips, staves and flails, more for bows, guns and thrown weapons, with line of sight required. Skills carry their own range
- a combatant that steps into water swims, and swimming costs more movement per tile

Round order: party and enemy troop interleaved by agility, then any townspeople who joined, then the world step, where every roaming monster, townsperson and your pet take one tile at once. Nothing outside the fight moves at any other time.

combatSummons.title: Summons
combatSummons.description:
A summon is a temporary fourth party member. In battle it exists for that battle only: never saved, never in the menu, gone when the fight ends or when you can no longer pay for it.

What can be called: a creature, a person the party has marked, the pet on your leash, a reflection of the summoner, or a revenant of a traveller you lost. Each rite draws only from its own kind.

Numbers are re-cut against your party's median and the level of the troop on the field, then multiplied by the rite's share: a familiar is half a traveller, a titan slightly more than one. Shape is kept, so a bruiser stays a bruiser. Two exceptions: the petrodemon, held by your oil, and the elder entity, which arrives with its own numbers and drains the summoner in about three turns.

Upkeep by kind:

- HP: demons, undead, shadows, swarms, titans
- MP: elementals, celestials, fae, the void
- AP: the reflection
- euros: constructs, war machines, dragons, champions
- soul: spirits
- oil: the petrodemon
- fixed few turns: beasts, verdants, familiars, called people

When you cannot pay, it leaves. A summoner who cannot pay in blood is left at 1 HP.

The familiar belongs to one character. The class of the caller decides which creature answers, its name is rolled once from the caller's name, and it is measured against their stats and level. Changing class remakes the pact. The first call adds it to the Followers page.

While a summon is out, a hyper bar fills with damage the party deals, one hit adding at most a third. Full, the summon fires its ultimate and the bar empties. The ultimate depends on the party's median level in brackets of ten, growing in damage, widening to the whole enemy line and adding effects at higher brackets. Damage is capped as a fraction of each target's maximum HP.

A summon is always computer controlled and has no 1 HP protection.

Outside a fight the same rites work, and what they call walks in a trailing slot. Each point of MP paid buys a fixed number of steps; when they run out, the binding ends. It joins any fight you enter at the stature it was called with.

combatArena.title: The Arena
combatArena.description:
The arena fights for its own sake, in two shapes:

- gauntlet: a run of fights in a chosen level bracket
- biome trial: a run against the fauna of a chosen biome

The party is rescaled to the bracket. A random roster can be fielded instead of your own.

Wins build a streak. The streak pays ascending money and items the further it goes, in the gauntlet and in single arena fights.

combatBulletHell.title: Bullet Hell Sequences
combatBulletHell.description:
Some fights break into a bullet hell sequence: you steer a small craft, dodge the enemy's pattern and shoot back.

Damage taken and dealt there counts in the fight.

combatSpirits.title: Spirit Battlers
combatSpirits.description:
Defeated enemies join a spirit roster. One of them can be fielded in place of an ordinary battler, at a cost that scales with what it was.

The feature runs on its own switch. A world with it disabled fights ordinary battles.

combatMimic.title: Mimicry
combatMimic.description:
Six mimic skills copy other bodies:

- Partial mimicry: the enemy's face and map sprite. Numbers unchanged
- Full mimicry: stats, HP, MP, AP, skills, body archetype and looks
- Mirror: re-executes the last skill the enemy used, against the enemy
- Copy ally: a companion's name, class, skills, sprite and body
- Random: full mimicry of a creature drawn at random
- Mutation: merges two random archetypes into your own body parts

All six need exactly one enemy on the field. Copying a body copies its limbs, which changes what you can hold and where you can be hurt.

combatThrow.title: Throwing Things
combatThrow.description:
Items, weapons and armour can be thrown up to eight tiles, diagonals included, with flight simulated from the item's weight. Heavy items travel a short distance and land hard.

A thrown item stays where it lands and can be picked up again by anyone.

combatCorpses.title: Corpses, Rewards and Cooldowns
combatCorpses.description:
After a fight the reward popup names everything gained at once: items in their rarity colours, money, experience and knowledge.

The dead leave corpses on the map. Enemy events are removed or locked behind a cooldown rather than respawning at once.

Knowledge is scaled by enemy level against the party median.

Every creature met is written into the Bestiary.

elementsOverview.title: Elements: How They Work
elementsOverview.description:
Nine damage types: Physical, Fire, Ice, Thunder, Water, Petro, Wind, Sacred, Cursed.

Every creature answers each type with a rate. Above 100% is a weakness, below is resistance, 0% is immunity, and a negative rate absorbs the element and heals from it.

The battle HUD prints what you have discovered about the enemy in front of you. The Bestiary keeps it.

States interact with elements: Wet raises lightning damage, Oily raises fire damage, Static absorbs lightning.

A class leans toward an element, and a weapon or modifier can carry one.

elementPhysical.title: Element: Physical
elementPhysical.description:
Edges, points, weight and fists. Most weapons deal it and most armour is built to stop it.

Physical damage severs limbs, breaks guards and lands holds. Heavy armour resists it and feeds Intimidation; light armour trades that for Stealth.

Spirits, oozes and gases resist it.

elementFire.title: Element: Fire
elementFire.description:
Applies Burned, which keeps dealing damage after the blow.

Raised against anything oily, dry or wooden. Resisted by the wet and the cold blooded, absorbed by things that live in fire.

elementIce.title: Element: Ice
elementIce.description:
Applies Cold, and Freeze at strength, which stops a body acting.

Raised against wet targets. Used on a burning target it removes the burn.

elementThunder.title: Element: Thunder
elementThunder.description:
Applies Static, and Paralysis at strength.

Devastating against a wet target. Absorbed by anything already Static, which heals it instead.

Machines and constructs usually resist it.

elementWater.title: Element: Water
elementWater.description:
Applies Wet, which raises lightning damage, lowers fire damage and is read by several states.

Its own damage is low.

petro.title: Element: Petro
petro.description:
Oil and what comes out of the ground with it.

Petro belongs to the petrodemons, which cannot be talked to, petted, recruited or reasoned with, and which drop barrels rather than coins. Oil works as a currency: it prices the post between worlds, it holds the petrodemon summon on the field, and the market trades it.

Petro damage leaves the target flammable.

elementWind.title: Element: Wind
elementWind.description:
Air, pressure and cutting motion. It unbalances and displaces.

Flying creatures deal it and resist it. It is weakest against rooted or heavy targets.

elementSacred.title: Element: Sacred
elementSacred.description:
Answered badly by the undead and the cursed. It is the one damage type that heals its target when that target is on the right side of the line.

Sacred workings usually carry protection and purging alongside damage. Several sit deep in expensive schools.

elementCursed.title: Element: Cursed
elementCursed.description:
Rot, ruin and draining. Dealt by the undead, answered by the sacred.

Cursed workings often cost more than MP, and the strongest are tagged Forbidden, which places them alone in the centre of their school's circle at a hundred times their value.

Efficient against the living. It heals the already dead.

worldMapPage.title: The World Map
worldMapPage.description:
The world map is one map of Europe. Each tile is a whole region. Walking one tile costs ten minutes of game time, two in a vehicle.

M cycles the display: hidden, corner minimap, fullscreen. In fullscreen, drag to pan, wheel or Q and E to zoom. Place names are drawn over their settlements.

Stepping onto a tile opens a travel choice: keep going, or visit the square, which builds its local map. T switches between the world map and the last local map.

Loose party members keep a two tile leash up there.

Squares marked "???" are adventures (own page).

worldProcedural.title: Procedural Maps
worldProcedural.description:
Almost every map is generated. A world map square becomes a map when you enter it, built from the world seed and that square's coordinates, so it is the same map every time you return.

What goes into one:

- the biome of the square, which sets the tileset and what grows there
- roads: straight runs, crossroads, T junctions and corners with centre lines. A road that leads nowhere loops back at the centre of the map
- rivers, wide and irregular, snapping to a fixed width at map borders so they continue into the next square. A river only reaches a border if the square beyond is water
- coastlines and beaches sampled along the border line, so neighbouring squares draw one continuous shore
- prefabs: hand authored 32x32 pieces dropped in, avoiding roads
- terrain features, single and multi tile, scattered by biome

Walking off the edge loads the neighbouring square's map directly, without returning to the world map.

worldBiomes.title: Biomes
worldBiomes.description:
The biome of a square sets its tileset, terrain features, fauna, music, weather and forageables.

Some biomes are special variants, rolled rather than fixed: spirit woods, crystal fields. Certain creatures live only in those, and a special biome map always places at least one of them, whatever the spawn mode or the calendar.

Roofed biomes, cellars, temple interiors, cave dens and dungeons, are entered through a structure entrance instead of walked into.

Biome names are printed through one service and read the same everywhere.

worldStructures.title: Structures Under the Map
worldStructures.description:
Entrances on procedural maps are walked into, not pressed. Stepping onto a grate opens it; walking into a cave mouth or a staircase opens that.

What lies behind is rolled per entrance tile from the world seed, the world square and the tile, so one stairway always leads to the same place.

- stairs down: any structure. Cellar, dungeon, crypt, catacombs, mine, cistern, warren, oubliette, library, forge, bunker, laboratory, shrine, tunnel, grotto, lava tube, barrow, station, salt works, cave den, temple
- stairs up: things built above ground and since buried. Temples, shrines, libraries, barrows
- cave: the cave family. Dens, frozen caves, crystal caves, fungal caves, lava tubes, sea grottoes
- grate: a sewer, and only in towns that declare one underneath
- hatch: a patron's vault, a cellar filled with money and rare weapons

The surface limits the options: ice fields hold frozen caves, a graveyard holds catacombs.

worldHouses.title: Houses, Inns and Shops
worldHouses.description:
Doors on procedural maps are handed to the building system. Pools of houses, inns, shops and tower blocks are seeded by coordinates, so a door is always the same business.

Buildings can have several floors and are configured as data. Shops and inns wear their name over the door.

Doors open with an animation when walked into. The lock is checked before the animation runs.

worldTerrain.title: Working the Terrain
worldTerrain.description:
Facing a terrain feature and pressing the action button offers to work it:

- trees: fell. Needs an axe in the inventory
- rocks: mine. Needs a war pick, any heavy weapon, or a chipped pickaxe
- plants: pick. Needs nothing
- anything: dismantle

The payout is crafting materials, the ones the workbench and the furniture builder use. Mining sometimes yields an ingot.

Foraging foliage, herbs and mushrooms always pays plant matter, and about two picks in five also pay an edible. What appears depends on the country: acorns and chanterelles in a forest, cloudberries on tundra, dates and prickly pear in a desert, cattail root and samphire on a marsh, blind mushrooms underground. The draw is weighted, and training Foraging raises the odds. Features that are a specific plant, wheat, corn, sunflower, cactus, kelp, reed, mushroom, pay that plant in any country.

Alien surfaces forage nothing. Their food comes from butchering local wildlife.

Felled trees and worked features stay gone when the map is rebuilt, including scenery inside a prefab: the same prefab standing elsewhere keeps its trees.

worldDungeon.title: The Dungeon and the Tower
worldDungeon.description:
One great dungeon, its layout rolled when the world is created.

Above ground it runs in ten levels, A to J, each of nine ordinary floors and one elevator floor. The elevator and the floor list jump to any floor already reached; unseen floors show as question marks.

Below ground is the lower tower, ninety two generated floors. Each is one of the structures from the procedural catalogue. Stairs read the other way down there: deeper is a smaller number, so descending goes from -21 to -22.

Every floor is checked for a valid staircase before use.

worldPuzzles.title: Puzzles
worldPuzzles.description:
Maps carry puzzles:

- sokoban blocks, pits that swallow them, goal tiles, reset shrines, an undo shrine
- pressure plates, timed plates that must be held, levers, gates wired with and / or logic
- ice floors, arrow tiles, conveyors
- crystal switches that flip sets of blocks between solid and open
- torches to light, sometimes timed, sometimes spreading fire
- colour tiles and lights out grids
- coloured doors needing a key item, combination locks
- warp pads, crackable walls, timed tiles, light beams to redirect, clones that copy your moves, magnetic objects, counterweights, floodable rooms

worldFog.title: Fog of War
worldFog.description:
Some maps are covered in fog, pushed back by walking. Vision is a cone, not a circle: you see where you face, and turning is how you look around.

Uncovered ground is remembered per map.

worldDigging.title: Digging and Secret Doors
worldDigging.description:
Some walls can be broken through at runtime, turning a dead end into a route. Digging is the deliberate version.

Secret doors look like wall until interacted with, then fade, make a noise and stay open.

Locked doors give three options: peek, pick, or break in. Peeking teleports you for a look without letting you move, and the menu that follows holds the other two. Picking plays a tetris minigame and needs lockpicks. Breaking in is filed as a crime.

worldMovement.title: Water, Climbing and Bridges
worldMovement.description:
Facing water and pressing the action button, or clicking an adjacent water tile, opens the water menu:

- swim: the sprite changes, companions are hidden, sprinting is disabled
- fish, with a rod in the party: pays random items, sometimes an encounter
- dive: goes under the surface

Climbable terrain is climbed slowly, facing up, with companions hidden and event interaction suppressed. Height is tracked; jumping down from three tiles or higher costs 5% health per tile fallen. Jumping north is an ordinary jump.

Bridges are layered. Enter from the approach and you walk on the bridge; enter from anywhere else and you pass under it. The layer holds across the whole span, companions included.

A mirror shows an upright reflection of whoever stands in front of it, and reflects events north of water.

worldWeather.title: Weather, Time and Seasons
worldWeather.description:
The clock starts at 8 AM on 1 January 2001 and never stops. Time advances as you walk and jumps when you sleep, wait or travel.

Weather is generated per country, seeded on the date, and changes on entering an outdoor map. The country sets sunrise and sunset, seasonal day and night temperatures, and which weather is possible.

- rain applies Wet
- storms apply Static
- snow applies Hot, from the body burning to stay warm

The screen is tinted by time of day and by temperature, blue for cold and red for hot. Indoors keeps the temperature tint and drops the time of day tint. Rain and night carry ambient sound on their own channel, layered over the map music.

worldDreams.title: Dreams
worldDreams.description:
Sleeping can drop you into a dream: a full 3D world rolled from a seed.

A dream deals four to seven regions and mixes them: backrooms, offices, escher stairs, drowned places, miniatures, cosmic voids, megastructures, car parks, hospitals, cathedrals, factories, datacentres, carnivals, sewers, tundra, desert, fleshpits, gardens, ruins.

Controls and rules:

- WASD walks, the mouse looks, space jumps. Holding jump while standing still takes off into flight
- the action button uses the weapon in your right hand; the d-pad or wheel steps a shuffled rack of every weapon in the game
- touching anything alive strobes and moves you to another dream
- walking head on into a wall, in one push or several, does the same
- drift regions change around you while you stand in them
- holes have no floor. Falling far enough leaves the dream

Every dream carries one to three laws: the ground breathes, gravity is light or crushing, colours invert, figures move only while unwatched, time hitches, nothing speaks alone, your size changes, the water rises and falls, the dream repeats itself.

The dream has no end: the ground loops in every direction and stacks upward as long as anyone climbs.

Every minute inside rolls a chance of knowledge, reported when you wake. Escape opens the wake up prompt: pinch your cheeks to wake, or keep dreaming.

worldAdventures.title: Adventures on the Map
worldAdventures.description:
Some world map squares carry a "???" marker, redrawn once a day. Stand on it, or face it from the next square, and choose Investigate to play a branching adventure written for that place.

Every choice leads somewhere and the last node pays out: a relic, gear, salvage, money, a fight with something native, a minigame, an augment, a change of faction standing, a crime filed against you, a rest that returns percentage points to everyone's needs, or nothing.

The party leader goes in, and the companion at their shoulder comments in their own register. Some choices are only offered to a leader of a particular temperament.

The prose is combinatorial and names the people who walked out there.

A biome carries one marker, two if it is very large, and a named place, country or hyperpower territory carries its own on top. An answered square stays answered. Everything done is written into the diary.

worldBologna.title: Bologna
worldBologna.description:
Bologna is in the game as itself, rasterised from OpenStreetMap into a grid of large cells that join seamlessly at their borders.

Every rasterised building has a door on its south face and every door is a way in. Most are homes; a share are shops and inns, seeded per cell and per tile, so a door is always the same business and wears its name.

The cells carry no hand placed events. The city is populated at runtime: townspeople drawn from the world's own faces and from Bolognesi born in the city, plus wildlife placed by habitat, street animals on pavements, park animals on green, waterfowl and fish in the canals, birds on rooftops.

worldPlatformer.title: Platformer Maps
worldPlatformer.description:
On a map tagged as a platform stage the controls become a side scroller: left and right walk, space jumps, shift runs, gravity pulls, and pressing jump against a wall wall jumps off it.

Ladders are climbed with up. Companions follow your exact path a moment behind, facing the way you faced.

worldFlying.title: Flying
worldFlying.description:
Flight moves you like an airship: freely, in any direction, over everything. Confirm lands you.

It is granted by particular items, skills and vehicles, not held permanently. Landing returns you to the rules of the terrain below.

worldConnections.title: The Map of Maps
worldConnections.description:
A second map shows every map you know and how they connect, built from the transfer events and doors between them.

Click a node to set it as destination and the shortest path is highlighted. A compass appears in the corner pointing at the next waypoint, and disappears on arrival or when the destination is cleared. The choice survives closing the map.

worldTreasure.title: Chests and Treasure Rooms
worldTreasure.description:
Chest contents are generated against the party's median level. An emptied chest stays empty, and open chests stay open.

Some maps hide treasure rooms: reachable, randomly placed rooms with heavier contents.

worldTechTree.title: Research and Discovery
worldTechTree.description:
Seven trees of discovery, one per discipline: Social Sciences, Alchemistry, Technomagica, Physics, Arcane, Mathematics, Astronomy, Theotecnical.

The scientific trees follow real progress from 2001 to 2012. Arcane and Technomagica follow the rediscovery of lost magic and its fusion with machinery. Theotecnical follows the Vatican rebuilding its dogma around engines. Each also carries fringe pseudoscientific branches and a few nodes generated from the world seed.

Completed nodes record the party leader who got there first.

Researching a node consumes crafting materials and returns most of that cost as refined byproducts.

travelOverview.title: Fast Travel
travelOverview.description:
Any place marked as a destination can be travelled to instead of walked to. Bus stops and signposts open the travel screen.

Choosing a destination and a mode puts you on a travel map for that transport, train, coach or taxi, with a countdown running while you are aboard. The timer keeps running while you open menus or fight, and survives scene changes. At zero you arrive.

Companions talk in transit, vehicle crews sleep in shifts, and the world clock keeps moving.

travelModes.title: The Thirty Ways to Travel
travelModes.description:
Each destination lists the transports that reach it. There are thirty, trading money against time.

Free or nearly free:

- walking: no cost, slowest
- bicycle: cheap, slightly quicker
- car sharing and camper: no money, fuel instead
- horse: cheap, better than a bicycle

Ordinary:

- bus, train, taxi, boat, ferry. The train is fast for its price, the taxi the same speed for twice as much

Expensive:

- economy flight, business flight, limousine, helicopter, private jet. A private jet is ten times walking speed
- cruise and submarine: slow, and the submarine is among the dearest
- balloon and zeppelin: slow and expensive

Exotic:

- magic carpet and dragon: very fast, very expensive
- teleport circle: twenty times walking speed for a modest fee, where one exists
- hypermetro, maglev, hyperloop
- starship, wormhole, quantum, time machine, dimensional. A dimensional crossing costs a thousand times the base fare and is a thousand times as fast

Cost is the base fare times distance. Speed divides the time.

vehiclesOverview.title: Owning a Vehicle
vehiclesOverview.description:
A vehicle is proven by an item. Holding the key, the deed or the broom puts that vehicle in the Vehicles menu and makes it summonable and drivable.

Vehicles are parked in the world, not carried. Each one's position is stored, including the world square and the underground layer. Where several are parked on one tile only the last is drawn, and interacting asks which you meant.

Walking up to a parked vehicle and interacting opens its menu: drive, enter the interior, use storage, refuel, repair.

The camper, the car and the starship have walk in interiors with storage holds.

vehicleCamper.title: Vehicle: The Camper
vehicleCamper.description:
The largest vehicle. One hundred litres of fuel, a walk in interior with beds and storage, repairable and upgradable, refuels at any roadside pump.

A ground vehicle, so it crosses road tiles on the world map faster than open country. Fast travel by camper costs fuel, not money.

Two workshop modules extend it:

- aquatic: it floats and dives. C dives and surfaces over water, and driving onto water floats it
- flight: rotors. F takes off and lands

Driving it opens a 3D scene (see the driving page). A crew lives aboard it (see the crew page).

vehicleCar.title: Vehicle: The Car
vehicleCar.description:
Faster than the camper and much smaller. Sixty litres of fuel, a small interior, repairable and upgradable, refuels at any pump. Takes the road bonus on the world map, and fast travel by car costs fuel rather than money.

Any parked car on the map can be stolen: face it, press the action button and choose to steal. That opens the lockpicking minigame and needs a lockpick, or a skeleton key, which opens it outright. Success gives you its keys and removes the car from the world. Failure files a vehicle theft against you and consumes the lockpick.

vehicleBike.title: Vehicle: The Bike
vehicleBike.description:
Human powered, so it needs no fuel and cannot run dry. The fastest vehicle available early, takes the road bonus, and has no interior, no storage and no repair costs.

No crew rota: the rider does everything.

vehicleBroom.title: Vehicle: The Flying Broom
vehicleBroom.description:
Needs no fuel, can be used indoors, and stows into your pack as an item.

It flies, so it passes over every tile of every map: walls, water, cliffs and events. It lands on anything that can be stood on, rooftops, cliff tops and bridges included, sets down where it hovers, and is boarded from the tile it landed on.

It takes no road bonus.

vehicleBoat.title: Vehicle: The Boat
vehicleBoat.description:
An inflatable dinghy. No fuel, no interior, no storage, no repairs, and it travels only on open water.

The party is drawn aboard it: everyone sits on the benches, bow first, facing the direction of travel, with the pet in the stern.

vehicleStarship.title: Vehicle: The Starship
vehicleStarship.description:
Two hundred litres of fuel and a full walk in interior. It cannot be refuelled at a roadside pump.

The hull, layout and appearance are generated procedurally from a set of trait axes and can be edited.

The starship needs no driver and flies itself, so its crew page covers living aboard rather than driving.

It is used from the star map (see the Galaxy pages).

vehicleFuel.title: Fuel
vehicleFuel.description:
The camper, the car and the starship burn fuel. The bike, the broom and the boat do not.

Fuel is bought at pumps at a price that moves with the world's oil market. The camper and the car fill at any roadside pump; the starship cannot.

Fuel is consumed by distance at a rate that differs per vehicle, and a fuel gauge sits in the corner while driving. Running dry strands you.

Fast travel by camper or car spends fuel instead of money.

vehicleRepair.title: Vehicle Damage and Repair
vehicleRepair.description:
A vehicle has twelve parts, each with its own health.

- critical, and they stop the vehicle dead when broken: engine, transmission, brakes, steering
- performance only: battery, alternator, radiator, fuel system, exhaust, suspension, tyres, body

Damage comes from what you hit. Hitting something soft marks the front only; hitting another vehicle at road speed is felt throughout. The damaged parts are named in the notification.

Repairs consume crafting materials, scaled by the depth of the repair. While riding, the vehicle's condition is drawn as an HP bar on the party HUD, with its fuel where a person's magic would be.

vehicleUpgrades.title: The Workshop
vehicleUpgrades.description:
Vehicles are upgraded with crafting materials at the workshop.

Four upgrades, three levels each:

- acceleration
- speed
- fuel capacity, unused by the bike and the boat
- structural health

Two one off modules, camper only:

- aquatic: floats and dives
- flight: rotors, take off and landing

Aerodynamic work reduces how much game time a world map tile costs.

Each level costs more exotic materials, from steel and plastic through titanium and circuitry to varlenian matter, nanotubes and quantum components.

vehicleCrew.title: The Crew
vehicleCrew.description:
The leader takes the wheel when a journey starts, and the HUD shows it. Only the driver earns the vehicle's specialization experience.

Time at the wheel is tracked per person as strain. Alertness is the party's sleep meter less that member's strain. Below 40% alertness the wheel passes to the best rested member above that line, and everyone not driving sheds strain. When nobody is fit to relieve the driver, they keep going and you are told.

Passengers sleep. Naps start below 40% sleep and run to full or to the end of the journey. Sleepers carry the Sleep state. They wake when the nap ends, when the party gets out, when someone enters the cabin, and on a crash, which also keeps them awake for the next hour.

The bike and the broom have no rota. The starship has no driver, and its crew tends one need at a time: a meal, a wash, a conversation, a game, a shift of sleep. Eating aboard consumes food from the hold, and an empty hold sends them to do something else.

vehicleDriving.title: Driving in 3D
vehicleDriving.description:
Driving the camper opens a 3D road scene built from the world map: the same grid of biomes, mountains as noise height fields, water flat and blue, roads as dual lane asphalt following the road tiles, everything else ground in that biome's colour, blended at the seams. Coastlines slope into the sea, and cities, forests and cacti are scattered along the way.

Three views, swapped with Tab or the pad's Y button:

- first person, behind an animated steering wheel and a working dash
- chase camera, with zoom on the wheel or the triggers
- cabin, a free roam view inside the vehicle, entered through a door

W throttles, Shift is turbo, S brakes and reverses, A and D steer, space is the handbrake, the mouse looks.

The driving model has a five speed automatic gearbox with an RPM engine note, lateral slip so the handbrake drifts, surface grip that differs between asphalt, dirt, grass, sand, snow and rock, gravity on slopes, and a chassis that follows the terrain.

Traffic runs nine models, hatchback, saloon, coupe, SUV, pickup, taxi, panel van, box truck and city bus, built at true size against the camper. They brake, take junctions and can be crashed into. A bus shoves harder than a hatchback.

On foot, the leader's weapon is in hand: click or press the shoulder buttons to swing it, and the d-pad steps through every weapon in the party's bags the leader can hold, changing their equipment.

Enemies matched to the biome idle by the roadside.

roadTraffic.title: Traffic, Roadkill and Theft
roadTraffic.description:
Map traffic is driven by the game rather than by event pages.

A car occupies as many tiles as its sprite is long, for every purpose: it never clips a wall it passes, cars collide bodywork against bodywork, and anyone under the bodywork is run over.

- only a moving car hits anything. A parked car is solid and harmless
- town traffic brakes for people, highway traffic does not

Being hit knocks you clear and triggers an accident. An NPC hit by a car takes injury conditions written onto their profile and readable on their health tab. A creature hit hard enough dies and leaves a harvestable corpse.

Driving over someone yourself injures them, drops their opinion of every party member, and files a hit and run. Ramming a creature flings it off the bonnet the first two times; from the third the odds it turns and fights climb steeply, and about five rams kill it. The damaged car parts are named.

Occasionally a car pulls over and its driver gets out, walks about, talks to people and later drives on. That driver is an ordinary wandering NPC, and the car sits parked and stealable meanwhile.

peopleOverview.title: People Are Real Here
peopleOverview.description:
Every person on the map carries a full profile, generated from their name and the world seed:

- a personality out of twenty five archetypes, which sets how they speak
- traits, the same ones your characters carry
- an ideology on five axes: economy, authority, tradition, militarism, mysticism
- wealth, skills, inventory and equipment
- a faction, a home, a job and a working schedule
- a backstory drawn from your world's history: the events they lived through, where and when they were born
- a medical history, including past diseases and badly healed bones

Part of the population is animals. Creatures are minted from the same system, and a creature on a beast class is non sentient: no conversation, no politics, no savings, no moving house, no starting money.

peopleEmpathize.title: The Empathize Panel
peopleEmpathize.description:
Talking to someone properly opens the Empathize panel: their identity, history, biology, health, romantic life, daily life, politics, and a log of their last conversations.
